payload.text: By Eric Francia How would you handle a junior employee questioning the way you’ve always done something? Might you roll your eyes and dismiss their comments as naivety? Or would you indulge their curiosity? As AI has made knowledge accessible on a scale never seen before, companies are becoming leaner and operating faster. What once took a large team months to do can now be done by a handful of people in a few days. It is undeniable that autonomous systems are changing the way we work. In the small and dynamic teams of the future, choosing the right humans to direct your AI systems will become make or break for a company. As a six-time founder, I’ve learned the best workplaces are the ones where questioning things is the norm. Here’s how to build a team that questions orders as much as it obeys them. AI by design Eric Francia, co-founder and CEO of Uniplay. “AI by design” doesn’t only mean building the right autonomous systems. It’s also about creating autonomous humans. You need to trust the human in the loop as much as you do the technology. The team around you ultimately shapes the company in ways you can’t control. So surrounding yourself with people you trust to make decisions when you’re not in the room is critical to success. The nature of job roles is changing. A job description can be totally different from the one advertised by the time you’ve found a candidate, and a six-month roadmap is outdated by the time you’ve finished drawing it up. The World Economic Forum has stated that 59% of employees will need to reskill by 2030 as AI reshapes the workplace. Hiring for a fixed set of skills won’t move the needle. The people worth investing in are those who are able to learn what comes next. Hire for curiosity Curiosity is the best trait you can hire for. When I look at a CV, it’s not just experience or academic credentials that draw me in. I look for what people have built on the side. What have they made on their own initiative? Hire for curiosity, and you’ll create an environment where people are willing to throw new ideas around and challenge outdated ways of doing things. If your team is worried about saying the wrong thing, they won’t end up saying the right thing either. In a world where technology is turning everything on its head, the companies that will thrive are the ones with curious people who are able to adapt to change quickly. Hand over real responsibility Employees with autonomy operate faster. They make better decisions because company vision is not abstract to people who are given real responsibility to drive it. Being involved in strategic direction stitches an employee into the fabric of the company and keeps them engaged. Trust your employees to know what isn’t working. Allow people to pursue new ideas and reinvent things. Your employees are likely to spot potential problems before you do when they’re closer to the product. Make sure your team has the autonomy to try to fix them before they take hold. Boredom is a big business risk As companies become smaller, employee retention is more important than ever. Losing your best people is costlier when you have fewer of them to begin with. The effects of a bored employee surface quickly in a small team. Boredom makes talented people a little bit slower, and a lot less likely to try the difficult thing. The challenge for modern leaders is keeping your team engaged and interested. A bored employee is more likely to be swayed by a flattering LinkedIn recruiter. Make sure to invest in development, keep your team learning, and always encourage curiosity. Give people autonomy and responsibility from the beginning, and boredom has nowhere to take hold. The mentality of risk and the drive to challenge something outdated is what you need to succeed in the changing work environment. Dare to be a beginner, and teach your team to do the same. That junior employee questioning how you’ve always done things could be the most valuable person in the room. Eric Francia is co-founder and CEO of Stockholm-based Uniplay , an agent-driven, game-based learning platform. He has experience building, exiting and scaling digital companies across 70 countries. Uniplay is his sixth company to date. Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: It’s an insecure world out there, and investors are responding by scaling up their cybersecurity spending. For the third quarter of 2026, global cybersecurity- and privacy-focused startups pulled in a total of $6.8 billion, per Crunchbase data. That’s up about 50% from the prior quarter and tied for the highest quarterly tally in years, as charted below. The funding bump was due to larger rounds, not more of them. Round counts actually declined sequentially across all stages last quarter, Crunchbase data shows. Biggest cybersecurity fundraisers AI startups accounted for the overwhelming majority of cybersecurity funding, with a particular focus on identity security. Overall, at least 18 companies at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity closed rounds of $100 million or more this past quarter. Of those, the largest funding recipient by far was enterprise identity security provider Keyfactor , which picked up $1 billion in a July growth round led by Summit Partners . Founded in 2001, the Ohio company isn’t exactly a startup, but it has attracted the bulk of its venture funding in the past 10 years and its pivot to AI is also of a more recent vintage. Dallas-based Island tied for second place with a $400 million September Series F led by Evolution Equity Partners . The startup, which offers tools for enterprises to see and govern how people and AI agents interact with applications and data, also secured a post-money valuation of $6.4 billion. Cyera , operator of an enterprise data security platform focused on AI agents, also announced a fresh $400 million Goldman Sachs Growth Equity -led investment in September, just three months after raising $600 million. The latest infusion set a $12 billion valuation for the New York startup. For a bigger-picture view of leading fundraisers, below we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 largest round recipients. Exits, too We also saw some good-sized acquisitions of cybersecurity startups this past quarter, even as the IPO market was fairly sluggish. Visa led the M&A pack with its $2.4 billion purchase of anti-fraud technology provider BioCatch in August. The acquisition is part of a broader effort by Visa to beef up its fraud detection and prevention capabilities for the AI age. Among private unicorns, meanwhile, Cyera proved it can find a way to spend a good chunk of the capital it raised. It acquired Oasis Security , an enterprise access management platform built for AI agents, in a deal reportedly valued around $1 billion. As for public offerings, Aura , which offers digital security services to consumers, was the lone sizable venture-backed market debut. The Boston-based startup completed an acquisition of an Australian public company, Qoria , in July, and then renamed the combined company Aura. Overall, an upbeat quarter Overall, Crunchbase funding data points to an upbeat environment for cybersecurity startup funding. This doesn’t seem particularly surprising given the steady drumbeat of worrisome news about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI technology. It’s not an especially reassuring time for most of us. But for cybersecurity founders, there’s certainly an ever-expanding array of hazards to keep at bay. We’ll keep watching in the current quarter to see if investment momentum continues to build. payload.text: While helping another founder build an app that collected information about class-action settlements, Zim Hang came to learn how challenging it can be for consumers to seek compensation from companies they believe wronged them. He also discovered mass arbitration, a way to pursue individual claims when companies’ contracts prevent customers from joining class actions. At the same time, he also realized that relatively few law firms were set up to manage thousands of those claims at once. Zim Hang, founder and CEO of Chariot Claims. (Courtesy photo) That gap became the basis for Chariot Claims , which has raised $10 million in Series A funding led by Silverton Partners to help consumers pursue claims over alleged privacy violations, hidden fees and subscriptions that are difficult to cancel. Indicator Ventures , Lightbank , Neon Fund , ZVC , Rosecliff Ventures , Alumni Ventures , FJ Labs , Graph Ventures and Vermilion Ventures also participated in the financing. The New York-based startup works with law firms to identify potential cases, find affected consumers and gather information needed to pursue compensation. The round brings its total funding to $15.7 million, which includes a $3.6 million seed investment in April 2025 and an earlier pre-seed round. Chariot’s latest round comes amid a surge in investment across legal tech. Funding to the legal tech space hit a record high last year, with $4.6 billion invested, per Crunchbase data . So far this year, legal tech startups have pulled in more than $3 billion, putting the sector on pace to match or exceed the 2025 total. The Chariot process works like this: For each case, consumers complete an intake questionnaire that assesses preliminary eligibility in real time. Chariot’s team then reviews these pre-qualified claims through a multi-layered system of technology and human oversight before sending it to the partner law firm handling the case. Hang, the company’s CEO, told Crunchbase News that Chariot typically receives more than 200,000 claim submissions per month and that it has taken on roughly 80 cases since shifting to its current business model just over a year ago. The company has about 15 employees and is currently breaking even, he said. It plans to spend the new funding primarily on hiring and product development, including AI tools to review cases and help determine whether consumers qualify to participate. A gap in consumer legal services Chariot is Hang’s third startup. His first company grew out of sleep research he conducted while studying psychology and neuroscience at Washington University . He turned that research into a smart-pillow business and later sold its intellectual property to a medical-device operator. He later worked in healthcare technology and fintech, founded a startup in the Web3 space, and then moved into legal technology. Across those industries, he said, he encountered complicated systems in which the interests of businesses and their customers did not always align. His experience helping the class-action settlement startup brought those concerns into focus. He described being “frustrated and mystified and horrified by how our justice system works.” Chariot started about three years ago, adopting its current model after Hang saw an opportunity to help law firms handle mass arbitration. Firms accustomed to class actions could struggle with the work required to manage large numbers of individual claimants, he said. “It’s just really inefficient for them to try to build workflows around 10,000 claimants or 100,000 claimants,” Hang said. Chariot handles parts of that administrative work, while its partner firms handle the legal claims. The startup charges the firms flat service fees, and they work on a contingency basis. Hang emphasizes that since it’s not a law firm, Chariot itself doesn’t file claims. It helps consumers pursue a variety of claims. Those claims include allegations that websites or apps tracked their information without consent, that companies added fees during checkout, or that businesses made subscriptions easy to start but difficult to cancel, for example. Finding evidence and drawing objections Chariot starts by looking for potential cases involving privacy violations, hidden fees and other consumer complaints. Its software scans public records, including federal court filings, and uses AI to analyze the allegations and prepare research for its partner law firms. That research includes legal memos based on publicly filed complaints. Chariot is also developing tools to track changes in laws and court decisions that could affect whether a case can proceed. The work remains in the early stages, with the goal of automating more of the research that associates and paralegals would otherwise do, according to Hang. Chariot reviews a few hundred potential cases each month, he said. It tests ads for about 30 potential cases to gauge whether it can find consumers who may have a claim, then selects roughly 10 to pursue more extensively with its partner law firms. Each case can involve many individual consumers, whom Chariot reaches through advertising and partnerships with consumer financial technology companies. To determine whether they have a claim, consumers must provide information to help assess it. For example, in the case of a data breach, that could be a notice from the company saying their information was exposed. For a hidden-fee complaint, it could include what they purchased, when they bought it, and how much they paid. Chariot is building AI tools to help review that supporting information and determine whether a consumer has a claim, according to Hang. The required evidence, and the difficulty of verifying it, varies by the type of alleged violation. The startup plans to make that step easier by allowing users to connect their email accounts so its software can look for relevant documents, rather than asking consumers to fill out forms.  Hang estimates that such improvements could help the company handle 10x to 100x its current claim volume. Companies push back Not everyone welcomes Chariot’s approach. Advertising for potential claimants has brought strong objections from some of the companies involved. In fact, Chariot has received cease-and-desist letters challenging, among other things, its use of company names and trademarks in ads, noted Hang. But he asserts that identifying those businesses is necessary to reach people who used their products or services. “As a part of our business, we need to mention the name of the company that has this alleged violation,” he said. Chariot reviews the letters with legal counsel and complies with demands it considers valid, Hang said. He declined to name specific companies for this article. His broader goal is to make alleged consumer abuses more costly for businesses. If more affected customers pursue compensation, he reasons, companies will have a stronger financial incentive to change those practices. “We want to make unethical unprofitable,” he said. Mike Dodd , general partner at Silverton, told Crunchbase News via email that his firm was attracted to Chariot’s vertical AI approach to working with law firms, which he called “exciting and defensible.” “It’s a greenfield market with space to expand horizontally and eventually into a generalized consumer legal AI solution,” he wrote. The firm was also drawn to what Dodd described as “a business model that aligns capitalistic incentives with access to justice.” “When a company breaks the law and breaks what it promises to its consumers, the consumer rarely seeks justice,” he added. “Chariot has built the technology to make individual consumer claims work at scale, and the team to operate it in a category where execution is genuinely hard.” Related Crunchbase query: Global Legal And Legal Tech Startup Funding In 2026 Global Venture Funding To AI Startups In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot , a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers. Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Jessica Herrin, CEO and founder of Marklo AI. (Courtesy photo) Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders. Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks. While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away , Clare V. , Monica + Andy , Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers . The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support. Planning campaigns To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems. Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive , Meta and Google , then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign. Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run. From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email. Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it. “Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking. In one case, Herrin described how Marklo identified a color trending on social media and a matching handbag a retailer had in stock but hadn’t promoted recently. It offered to plan a post based on one that had performed well before. Latico Leathers offers another example of how a brand uses Marklo. The company used the software to plan a month’s worth of marketing in one day, a process that had previously taken most of a week across meetings, spreadsheets and five tools, according to Herrin. In the end, humans review and approve Marklo’s proposed work. The company says it does not use customer data to train AI models. As for its revenue model, Marklo plans to charge a monthly subscription fee, with additional charges based on usage. For now, brands can install and try it for free. “I’m very passionate about small and medium businesses, and I want to make it accessible to every single brand that runs on Shopify,” Herrin told Crunchbase News in an interview, “so that they can operate like a big brand.” A change of direction The decision to build Marklo followed a change in how Herrin thought about Stella & Dot’s future. That company began as a way for women to earn money on their own schedules by hosting trunk shows in their own homes. It expanded into apparel and skincare and paid out more than $500 million to its sellers, Herrin said. “For me, it was never about the jewelry,” she told Crunchbase News. When COVID-19 put a stop to in-home gatherings, business dropped 80% almost overnight. Herrin also realized that women who might once have signed up to sell Stella & Dot products suddenly had other options. They could promote multiple brands as influencers or open their own Shopify stores. She described Stella & Dot as “the COVID victim that had pre-existing conditions.” Rather than rebuild the old model, Herrin sold the businesses and brands separately. Later, she bought back the Stella & Dot brand to sell through a different channel and test Marklo. She was also reconsidering what she wanted to do next. As she approached her 50th birthday, Herrin questioned whether she would choose to start the same business again. “As an entrepreneur, you don’t just start a business; you start a life,” she said. She still wanted to help people build businesses. What had changed was the problem she wanted to solve: Opening an online store had become easier, but managing its marketing still meant gathering information from several systems and coordinating the next campaign. “The mission was the same, but the solution needed to evolve,” Herrin said. A return to venture capital For Marklo, Herrin also returned to venture funding after relying more on profits to grow Stella & Dot. She had raised venture capital for her first company, which became WeddingChannel.com , but came away feeling that it had raised too much money. She took a different approach with Stella & Dot, building it with about $2 million in capital and a focus on profitability. “Here’s a new growth strategy,” Herrin recalled thinking. “How about profits?” With Marklo, she wanted to hire engineers and develop the software faster. Its 11-person team includes engineers who previously worked at Shopify and Google. She also sought investors with commerce experience. “Raising capital isn’t just about having money for expenses,” Herrin said. “It’s about bringing a brain trust together.” Experience as ‘the customer she’s building for’ Kirsten Green , founder and managing partner of Forerunner Ventures, said Herrin’s experience building Stella & Dot was a central reason for backing Marklo. “Jessica uniquely has been the customer that she’s building for right now at every stage, from starting a brand to having a brand at scale,” Green told Crunchbase News in an interview. That experience gives Herrin firsthand knowledge of where teams lose time, which decisions affect profitability and what brands need before trusting new technology, she added. While AI in general makes it easier to produce marketing content, Green sees the greater opportunity in helping brands decide on what exactly to promote, as well as in understanding the impact on margins and how to grow in ways consistent with their identity. Marklo, she said, incorporates the judgment needed to turn business data into useful recommendations. The opportunity comes as AI is taking a larger share of investment in the broader sales and marketing sector . Startups in sales, marketing and customer relationship management raised $7.5 billion across 830 rounds globally this year through mid-September, with most of that investment going to companies in Crunchbase’s AI-related categories. Funding is on pace to finish below 2025’s $11.1 billion, while deal volume could fall for a fourth straight year — a sign that investors are concentrating their bets in fewer companies. “It’s one thing to collect the information; it’s another thing to understand how to present it and how to recommend an action against it,” Green added. The investor also pointed to Marklo’s ability to serve businesses at different stages, noting that coordination becomes more complex and information harder to share as brands grow. As such, the prospect of software that can grow alongside its customers was another draw. Green said she also valued Herrin’s decision to develop Marklo alongside brands already using it, giving the company customer feedback before its broader launch. “I like the fact that she built this product while it was being used,” she said. payload.text: By Daniel Kjellén A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary. Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause. For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on. Lessons from the front line Daniel Kjellén, CEO and co-founder of Freda. After selling my first venture, Tink , to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing. Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours. A problem with too many heads Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another. Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget. “Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one. Why the second time is different In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder. The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you. Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it. Maximum viable product Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink. We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs. You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet. Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda , the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022. Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: A total of 38 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in September, adding $71 billion in value to the board. Semiconductors, financial services and space technology led for new counts with the remainder hailing from a broad swath of industries including biotech, AI infrastructure, AI training, security and frontier labs. Twenty-one of last month’s new unicorns are U.S. headquartered. Six new unicorns joined the board from China and three from the U.K., while Canada, Saudi Arabia, Japan, Israel, Italy, Finland, Germany and Bulgaria each added one new unicorn. Through September, 311 companies have joined the board so far this year, putting 2026 on track to be the second-highest year for new unicorn creation, following only the venture peak year of 2021, when counts topped 600. Several companies already on the board stand out for significant valuation increases via new raises last month. They include San Francisco-based Cognition , developer of AI for software engineering, which saw its value climb to $48 billion, up from $26 billion only four months earlier. Data center provider Crusoe was valued at $31 billion last month, up from $10 billion a year ago. And Paris-based frontier lab Mistral was valued at $24.4 billion in its more recent funding, up from $13.7 billion a year ago. New unicorns in September Here are September’s 38 new unicorn companies: Semiconductors Fab2 , an Austin-based semiconductor manufacturing startup, closed a $500 million Series A at a $3.7 billion valuation, led by Fundomo . The 3-year-old company builds compact chip factories and develops their manufacturing equipment internally, aiming to make semiconductor production more accessible. Celero Communications , an Irvine, California-based semiconductor company, raised a $275 million Series C, valuing it above $3 billion and bringing total funding to $415 million. Atreides Management , Valor Equity Partners and CapitalG led the round. The 2-year-old company develops digital signal processing chips for high-speed optical connectivity in AI infrastructure. Micronano Core , a Hangzhou-based AI chip developer, announced a $149 million Series C. Its IoT inference chips combine memory and computing to reduce power consumption and data movement. The 5-year-old company was valued at $1 billion. Evas Intelligence , a Beijing-based AI chip company, raised $298 million at a valuation of $2.2 billion. The 4-year-old company develops AI computing chips using the open RISC-V architecture. SiMa.ai , a San Jose, California-based developer of specialized AI chips and software, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, co-led by Fidelity and Amplify Partners , bringing total funding to $500 million. The proceeds for the 8-year-old company will support its software platform and next-generation hardware for robots, vehicles and drones. Financial services OG , a Texas-based prediction-market platform, announced a strategic partnership with Robinhood , which will take an equity stake following OG’s separation from Crypto.com . The less than 1-year-old company was valued at $5 billion. The investment amount was not disclosed; the partnership will route Robinhood event-contract trading through OG’s regulated exchange and clearing infrastructure. Saudi Arabia-based Barq , a digital payments company, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion valuation. Investors included Noon Investments , Sohar International and M20 Capital . The 3-year-old company has processed more than $117 billion in 2 years. Ridgeline , a Nevada-based financial software company, raised a $250 million Series E at a $1.43 billion valuation led by founder and chairman Dave Duffield . The 8-year-old company provides an AI-based investment management platform for asset and wealth managers. Félix , a Miami-based remittance platform for Latino immigrants operating through WhatsApp , secured $200 million in financing: an $87 million Series C equity round led by Andreessen Horowitz valued at $1.4 billion and $113 million in debt from General Catalyst ’s Customer Value Fund. The 5-year-old company plans to expand to lending and add to its Latin American reach . Space technology Munich-based space company The Exploration Co. raised a $450 million Series C, co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners , Atomico and EQT at a valuation of $2 billion. The financing for the 5-year-old company will advance its reusable Nyx spacecraft for an International Space Station mission and support development of its Storm rocket engine. Hubble Network , a Seattle-based satellite connectivity company, raised a $200 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Smith Point Capital , bringing total funding to approximately $300 million. The 5-year-old company enables standard Bluetooth devices to connect directly to satellites for tracking and sensor-data applications. Oxfordshire, U.K-based Open Cosmos , a satellite company, secured $346 million, co-led by ETF Partners and Lightrock , valued at $1 billion. The 11-year-old company manufactures satellites and provides infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation and intelligence services. Bulgaria-based EnduroSat , a satellite company, raised $205 million in a round co-led by Riot Ventures and Atreides Management , reaching a $1 billion valuation. The 11-year-old company has raised financing that will expand standardized spacecraft production, including new manufacturing capacity in the U.S. and Europe. Biotechnology and medical devices Alzheon , a Framingham, Massachusetts-based developer of treatments for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders, raised around $79 million. The   13-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. Investors were not disclosed. Shanghai-based Anew Labs , an AI drug discovery company, raised $290 million at a $1.5 billion valuation following its spinoff from ByteDance . HSG , IDG Capital , Hillhouse Capital and 5Y Capital co-led the round. Anew develops tools for biomolecular prediction and drug discovery; ByteDance retained a 56% stake. Precision Neuroscience , a New York-based brain-computer interface developer, closed a $250 million Series D, bringing total funding to $430 million and reaching a valuation of approximately $1 billion. Pershing Square and Ackman Oxman Institute led the round. The 5-year-old company is building a brain–computer interface that is minimally invasive and removable. Toronto-based Biossil , a biotechnology company, raised $153 million at a $1 billion valuation led by the OpenAI Startup Fund , with participation from Founders Fund and other investors. The 3-year-old company uses AI to identify abandoned drug candidates that could succeed under different treatment approaches. The financing will expand clinical development and support additional drug acquisitions. AI and internet infrastructure Gimlet Labs , a San Francisco-based AI cloud infrastructure company, raised a $300 million Series B at a $3 billion valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz . The 3-year-old company distributes AI inference workloads across different types of chips to improve performance and efficiency. It announced in March that its customers include one of the leading frontier labs. Helsinki-based Verda , an AI cloud company, raised a $189 million Series B led by Emergence Capital . The financing valued the 6-year-old company above $1 billion with total funding over $450 million. The company manages physical data centers along with its cloud platform. London-based CDN77 , an internet infrastructure company supporting content delivery for large streaming, gaming and software companies, raised $570 million in its first external financing led by CVC Capital Partners . The 15-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. AI training Micro1 , a San Francisco-based AI training-data company, raised more than $100 million led by Dream Ventures at a $4 billion valuation, an eightfold increase from its valuation in September 2025. The 4-year-old company recruits and vets specialists who create training and evaluation data for AI developers. Forbes reported that participants included two frontier AI laboratories and two x.AI co-founders. AfterQuery , a San Francisco-based provider of expert-created AI training data, reached a $3.2 billion valuation in September, more than 10x its valuation five months earlier, according to Forbes . The funding amount and lead investor were not publicly disclosed. The 1-year-old company’s datasets capture professional reasoning in fields such as software engineering, law and finance. AfterQuery was part of the Winter 2025 Y Combinator batch. Robotics and autonomous driving Shanghai Zaofu Intelligent Technology , the Shanghai-based operator of Hello’s robotaxi business, raised about $100 million at a valuation close to $3 billion. Shanghai State-owned Capital Investment fund led the round. The financing to the 1-year-old company will support a 10,000-GPU computing cluster, AI model development and commercialization of Level 4 autonomous driving. Lyte AI , a Sunnyvale, California-based robotics perception company, raised a $165 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Maverick Silicon . Founded by former Apple and PrimeSense engineers, the 5-year-old company combines custom chips, sensors and spatial software to help robots perceive their surroundings. The financing will accelerate deployments across logistics, manufacturing and inspection applications. Health insurance Angle Health , a San Francisco-based health benefits company, announced a $200 million Series C at a $2.7 billion valuation. Vitruvian Partners led the financing. It also includes $400 million in secondary financing for existing investors. The 7-year-old company provides a benefits platform using AI to make healthcare more affordable for small and midsize employers. The company services 5,000 businesses. Thatch , a San Francisco-based health benefits platform, raised a $108 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation. Investors included The General Partnership , Index Ventures , General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz . The 5-year-old company helps employers provide individualized health budgets for employees to select their own medical plans. It has 5,000 employers utilizing its service. Energy and EV infrastructure China-based NIO Power , a battery-swapping and charging company, agreed to a strategic transaction that gives Geely Auto a 30% stake. Geely will contribute its Yiyi battery-swapping operation and a $95 million investment. The 9-year-old company was valued around $2.4 billion. TAR , an Austin-based developer of off-grid power systems for AI data centers, raised a $120 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation, led by Spark Capital . The less than 1-year-old company builds modular systems for renewable energy and battery systems as data-center operators seek access to electricity. AI applications Brahma AI raised $150 million led by Multiples , at a valuation just over $2 billion. The 3-year-old company, headquartered in London with offices in Los Angeles and Mumbai, built an enterprise audiovisual content platform for media, advertising, sports and healthcare customers. The financing will support research, commercial expansion and a larger Silicon Valley presence. Sequen , a New York-based AI ranking and personalization company, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.44 billion valuation, led by Prysm Capital . The 2-year-old company’s software helps enterprises respond to customer behavior in real time, improving the relevance of recommendations. Cybersecurity Rome-based Exein , a cybersecurity company protecting connected devices and autonomous machines, raised $270 million at a $1.7 billion valuation, led by Headline . The financing to the 8-year-old company will support U.S. and Asia-Pacific expansion and development of AI security models. Tel Aviv-based Guardio , a consumer cybersecurity company, raised $40 million at a $1.1 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $167 million. Wiz co-founder Assaf Rappaport joined existing investors including Ion Crossover Partners and Union Tech Ventures , among others. The 8-year-old company protects consumers against phishing, scams, malicious websites and AI-generated fraud. AI models Beijing-based Naive AI , a language-model startup, raised $120 million reaching a valuation of $1.4 billion. Investors include Tencent , IDG Capital , Matrix Partners China and HSG . The less than 1-year-old company raised $400 million across three rounds so far this year, before releasing its first public model. Arcee AI , a San Francisco-based developer of open-weight foundation models, announced a $150 million Series B led by Vista Equity Partners , Cambium Capital Partners and Emergence Capital , valuing the company above $1 billion. The financing will support the 3-year-old company’s Trinity models and products for customizing and operating them. Manufacturing and construction software CADDi , an AI company for manufacturing with dual headquarters in Tokyo and Chicago, raised a $114 million Series D at a $1.2 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $234 million. Investors included Moore Strategic Ventures and Coreline Ventures . The 9-year-old company’s platform organizes design and procurement and production; the financing will deepen its technology and accelerate North American expansion. Kahua , a Georgia-based construction software company, secured a growth investment of $250 million led by Bain Capital Tech Opportunities , valuing it above $1 billion. The 17-year-old company manages construction projects, with the investment supporting its AI capability build out and commercial growth. Defense technology Covenant , a Washington, D.C.-based defense company, emerged from stealth with $250 million raised across three rounds at a valuation above $1 billion. The 2-year-old company develops long-range cruise missiles with manufacturing in Texas, Germany and Israel. Backers who have led across three rounds include Andreessen Horowitz , Founders Fund , Lux Capital , 8VC 1 , Lightspeed Venture Partners and Aleph . Food Medici Brands , the New York-based parent of consumer food brands David Protein and HallPass, raised a $250 million Series B at a $2.25 billion valuation. Greenoaks and Valor Equity Partners co-led the round. The financing to the 2-year-old company will expand retail distribution, develop new products and support additional brands. payload.text: By Nnamdi Okike You have likely never heard of Tosin Eniolorunda . You should have. Over the past decade, Tosin and his team built Moniepoint into the operating system for more than 6 million Nigerian businesses, processing over $300 billion a year , or 39% of Nigeria’s digital payments volume and 8 out of every 10 in-person payments . As a Nigerian American, I’ve witnessed my father make trips to Western Union to send money back home for decades, and I experienced Nigeria’s fee-laden payment system when visiting the country. Moniepoint is transforming that system. Nnamdi Okike, co-founder and managing partner of 645 Ventures. Moniepoint is not alone. Sea Limited , Grab , Kaspi , Yassir , Nubank 1 — these are companies most Americans have never heard of, despite them being worth several tens or hundreds of billions, following the trail blazed by Tencent , Alibaba and MercadoLibre . These are super apps that bundle banking, commerce, ride-hailing and bill pay into one trusted application. The idea never took hold in the U.S. for one reason: trust is cheap here. With 96% of households already banked , a specialist app inherits the credibility of the financial system. Where trust is cheap, there is no need for a super app. Build trust first In emerging markets, trust is the whole problem. Four conditions tend to precede a super app: High mobile penetration, which makes distribution cheap; weak incumbent competition; poor existing financial services; and the condition most investors screen past, a financial crisis severe enough to strip incumbents of legitimacy. These populations are not merely underbanked. They were harmed, and the institutions that harmed them still hold the market. Brazil froze roughly 80% of bank deposits and financial investments for 18 months in 1990 in an effort to break hyperinflation. The banking consolidation that followed left five banks holding about 80% of banking assets and charging card rates north of 300% . That was the void Nubank was born into. Kazakhstan went through it twice: savings erased by inflation in the thousands of percent when the ruble zone collapsed in 1993, then a 2007–09 banking crisis in which the country’s largest bank, BTA, holding roughly a quarter of the system’s assets, was nationalized and defaulted amid allegations of multibillion-dollar fraud. Kaspi grew into that void. Southeast Asia’s 1997 crisis was harsher still. Indonesia closed 16 banks in a single announcement, the rupiah lost about 85% of its value, and output fell 13 %. Two decades later roughly half of Indonesian adults still had no bank account, which enabled Sea to build Shopee and SeaMoney into that gap. Kaspi also answers the objection I hear most from American investors, which is that these markets are too small to produce large exits. Kazakhstan has only 20 million people, and according to company filings , around 14 million — nearly 70% of its population — use Kaspi. The average user transacts roughly 77 times a month . It earns $9 billion of revenue at 56% EBITDA margins, and its enterprise value is over $17 billion . Depth of spend, not population, sets the ceiling. Compare Nubank to Chime . Nubank has 14x the customers, 127 million to Chime’s 9.5 million , about 7x the revenue and a market capitalization more than 6x larger. Nubank has brought over 31 million previously unbanked Brazilians into the financial system . A technology applied in an overlooked market with a large unaddressed pain point can build a bigger and more defensible company than the same technology applied in a rich one. Screen for the four conditions and a few markets stand out as places where the next super app could emerge: Bangladesh: Five banks looted from the inside for years before the 2024 change in government exposed them , with the government now promising to pay 7.5 million savers whose money is gone. Egypt: Repeated devaluations of the pound between 2016 and 2024, shrinking savings held at banks the state itself owns. Vietnam: Savers pulled 80% of deposits out of one major bank in 2022 after its owner was arrested in a $24 billion fraud. Pakistan: A near-default and 38% inflation in 2023 , then government-built rails and a national ID that makes onboarding nearly costless. One boundary condition: The crisis must be severe enough to delegitimize incumbents but contained enough that the currency and payment rails still work. The first generation of super apps created enormous value for the investors who backed them early. In 2001, the South African media company Naspers paid roughly $34 million for a 46.5% stake in Tencent, a stake later worth more than $100 billion and one of the best tech investments ever made . Sequoia Capital ’s investment in Nubank’s $2 million seed round, combined with its lead Series A investment, was worth $7 billion at the company’s IPO . The second generation is scaling now. The third will be built on stablecoins and AI technologies, in Abidjan, Buenos Aires, Karachi and Lagos, by founders like Tosin Eniolorunda who will play an increasingly important role in the growth of emerging market economies. Nnamdi Okike is co-founder and managing partner of 645 Ventures , where he oversees the firm’s investing strategy, governance and compliance, with a focus on fintech and enterprise technology. Since co-founding 645 Ventures in 2014, he has invested in and partnered with companies including RentSpree , Setpoint , Sequence , Solidus Labs , Order and Uptiq . Previously, he was an investor at Insight Partners , where he invested in 19 companies and had nine exits representing more than $9 billion in exit value. Illustration: Dom Guzman Full disclosure: The author owns shares in Kaspi, Sea Limited and Nubank. None of the companies mentioned are portfolio companies for his firm, 645 Ventures. ↩

payload.text: Brendan Wallace has spent much of the past decade investing in technology that impacts how real estate is bought, built and managed. Now, the Fifth Wall co-founder sees AI changing the kinds of companies worth backing and expanding the definition of proptech itself. Founded in 2016, Los Angeles-based Fifth Wall has grown into one of the largest investment firms focused on real estate technology, with roughly $3 billion in commitments and capital under management. Its portfolio includes Procore , OpenDoor , Blend and Hippo . Notable exits include ServiceTitan , which went public in 2024, and flexible workspace provider Industrious , which real estate giant CBRE took full ownership of in January 2025 at a valuation of more than $800 million. Major real estate and hospitality companies — including CBRE, Hines , Hilton and Marriott — are among its investors, giving the startups it backs a direct connection to potential customers. Wallace, who serves as CEO and chief investment officer, brings experience on both sides of that relationship. He worked in real estate finance at Goldman Sachs and Blackstone before co-founding workforce analytics startup Identified , which was acquired by Workday in 2014, and ridesharing company Cabify . As AI makes certain products easier to replicate, Wallace sees growing potential in startups that use technology to own and operate real estate themselves. In a recent interview with Crunchbase News, we discussed that shift, why proptech funding totals may overlook some of the sector’s biggest investments, what it all means for founders, and the housing problems he believes still need solving. This interview has been lightly edited for brevity and clarity. Crunchbase News: Our recent proptech funding analysis showed capital on pace to roughly match or slightly exceed last year , but across fewer deals. What does that tell you about the market? Brendan Wallace, CEO and chief investment officer of Fifth Wall. (Courtesy photo) Brendan Wallace: My sense is that statistic might belie the actual amount of funding flowing in, because what was previously characterized as proptech in the narrowest sense is probably representing a smaller share of where proptech investors are deploying capital. There are increasingly horizontal solutions that are just as good, if not better, than many of the vertical solutions we’re seeing. We recently made a very big investment out of our growth fund into Higgsfield , the visualization software company. Most people reflexively think of that as being for movies or rendering scenes. But we saw real estate agents and commercial leasing brokers using it to represent spaces. For an unbuilt home, you could feed it blueprints, have it build an entire home, put your family inside and walk through it in a full scene. That had surpassed the industry-specific solutions for space visualization that would have been narrowly defined as proptech. Another category is investment flowing into full-stack businesses: real estate companies themselves. We just invested $135 million into Atoms , and I would be surprised if that fell under the definition of proptech. Those are probably the two categories that might not be captured: horizontal software, with Higgsfield as an example, and businesses that reimagine physical space based on autonomy, AI or robotics. They’re actually building a physical thing. They’re building a real estate company, directly or indirectly. How much is AI driving that shift toward software that serves multiple industries? Wallace: It’s a big part of it. Without something profoundly better that you can’t replicate on your own, there’s less justification for buying outside software. There still is a justification, to be clear. There’s just less of one. No real estate company can build the kind of visualization software Higgsfield has. I don’t believe they ever will. But a tenant engagement app they might have previously purchased and rolled out to their assets, they can now replicate over a long weekend. The imperative to buy these third-party solutions has been reduced, and more value has been placed on the best horizontal solutions, whether that’s a foundation model or a specific use case like sound, audio or visual. I don’t know the statistic, but it would be interesting to know how much real estate companies are spending on foundation models versus proptech applications. If I had to guess, we’re probably close to, or at, an inflection point where it’s passing it. No one would characterize Anthropic as a proptech company, but it might be taking a significant amount of the upstream proptech dollars, and an even larger share downstream once you go through the application layer. Has AI reset the bar for what makes a venture-scale proptech software company? What does a startup need beyond adding AI to existing workflows? Wallace: We’re still figuring that out, but I think it has to be something that can’t be replicated. Anything where the intellectual property moat is not extremely defensible is very challenged, and I think it will be for some time. Simple application point solutions are becoming less financeable by venture investors because the capacity of one of the large labs to build that as an interface, or of a company to build it on its own, has caught up so dramatically. The flip side is that bespoke AI development labs are now building solutions for the real estate industry. We backed one called Antares , which is kind of like a Palantir for real estate. Antares works with a number of our strategic limited partners. They go in-house, identify a problem they think can be solved with an AI-based solution, build the intellectual property specifically for the organization, and leave it with them. It’s more of a fee-for-development model than an intellectual property licensing model. You’re seeing that across industries, and you’re absolutely seeing it in real estate. In some sectors, founders argue that domain expertise gives specialized AI companies an advantage over broad models. How durable do you think that advantage is? Wallace: I’m a little more optimistic about foundation models’ and general intelligence’s capacity to adapt rapidly to specific use cases. I wouldn’t argue that specific legal expertise, for example, is not valuable. But I think that moat collapses over time. You might be on a treadmill. Think about what ChatGPT looked like in 2023 versus what Claude looks like today. At a basic level, it’s the same thing, but they’re totally different things. The sophistication, memory, capacity to be personalized, and ability to build off natural language instructions are unlike anything I think anyone could have anticipated in 2023. What will that look like in 2029? I think what you’re saying is true today. It’s less true than it was, and it might become even less true in three years. Is construction technology still an area of focus for Fifth Wall? Wallace: It is, but it’s less of a focus today. When we look at our performance, it has generally favored two things: pure software businesses, whether marketplaces, consumer software or enterprise software, and full-stack businesses. Anytime you get into physically doing things, the risk profile changes pretty profoundly. I don’t think it should be surprising that construction tech broadly is probably the biggest graveyard in all of venture. Maybe there’s a bigger category, but if there is, it’s not obvious to me. Why do you think construction tech continues to attract significant funding? Wallace: Because it’s still a massive market and a huge problem. If someone can bring greater efficiency to construction, you’re talking about one of the largest markets on earth. It’s such a massive prize that the largest funds are going to focus on it. For founders raising seed or Series A funding, what opportunities would you encourage them to pursue that might not have been fundable a few years ago? Wallace: You can actually build new real estate companies. That hasn’t really been conceptualized as being within a venture mandate, but it’s absolutely something we’d like to see. For example, we have a better approach to buying multifamily assets, stripping out costs, and running more of the processes, operations and management with AI. That’s something I think is eminently fundable today by Fifth Wall and many venture funds. I don’t think that would have been the case five years ago. I’d encourage founders to look at building full-stack, capital-R real estate businesses. The second opportunity is around data. Real estate is characterized by extremely opaque data in a way that’s different from most large financial markets. Nothing that’s happened in proptech in the past 10 years has fundamentally changed that. Where can generative AI provide signal through that opaque data to make capital allocation decisions? Real estate is generally a cash-flowing asset. We don’t necessarily think of it as comparable to bonds or stocks, but it is, and it should be. Can you derive signal by looking at more data or different data, or use generative AI to predict what kind of real estate will perform better? The quantitative model that has existed for securities for a very long time now has the potential to affect real estate, because we have computational capacity that wasn’t previously possible. Are there opportunities you’re interested in that have less to do with AI? Wallace: We’re intrigued by the intersection of land, real estate and the financial instruments around them. To make most of what we describe as real estate, you usually have to build something on land. Land is an input to almost all real estate, but many real estate owners don’t want to own it or take on that risk profile. Is there a way to decouple having to own land from owning and operating a building? That’s less about AI and more about financial engineering. There are new financial solutions emerging in that category that interest us. How could AI, robotics and autonomy change the kinds of real estate businesses founders build? Wallace: I’m interested in entrepreneurs who can conceptualize real estate through a sociological lens: New catalysts are changing how humans use space compared with the past. That’s happened for a long time. E-commerce built the modern industrial real estate industry. Cloud computing, the internet and now AI built the data center industry. Cell towers were born out of mobile phones and smartphone technology. Genome sequencing helped create the lab-space real estate asset class. I think we’re on the precipice of three new catalysts that will spawn entirely new real estate asset classes: AI, robotics and autonomy. In many ways, they’re entangled. Do you expect fewer dedicated proptech venture firms? What would that mean for founders? Wallace: I do think you’re going to see fewer vertical funds, in the narrowest sense of where we started this conversation. Dedicated venture capital funds investing in consumer and enterprise software focused on an industry —– I think you’ll see less of that, and funding will probably continue to go down in that category. The inverse is venture capital funding real estate businesses themselves. I think that’s about to explode. If you were starting a company in this sector today, what problem would you most want to solve? Wallace: Housing drives everything. Housing costs drive our economy, and the U.S. is grappling with a very real housing affordability crisis. It’s unclear how to solve it. There are multiple approaches. One is building homes better, faster and cheaper — that’s construction tech. Another is financing homes at a lower cost. How do you bring efficiency to the housing finance market? That’s a place where we’ve made a lot of money and invested a lot, but I would argue it’s still unsolved. Getting a mortgage is still painful, archaic, slow and too expensive. Related to that is making regulation more efficient to improve housing affordability. That’s not something an entrepreneur can solve alone, but there’s potential to bring efficiency to how cities deal with this problem. There’s an intersection of regulatory technology, policy work and consulting. How do we make it so more people can afford homes in the cities they live in? That problem isn’t going away. Despite everything that’s happened, housing has gotten more expensive, not less. Axiom Solutions International , $2B, cloud and power infrastructure: Axiom Solutions International, a private cloud and power infrastructure company spun out of manufacturing services provider Flex , secured $2 billion in new financing. General Catalyst and Koch Equity provided the strategic investment by purchasing shares of Austin-based Axiom from Flex at an initial enterprise value of $37.5 billion. Flex says it plans to separate Axiom into an independent publicly traded company early next year. 2. TypeSafe AI , $870M, foundational AI: TypeSafe AI, developer of Jev, a recently launched AI model with a large and growing early following, raised $870 million in new funding with Andreessen Horowitz as the largest investor, according to a Bloomberg report . Sequoia Capital also participated in the round, which reportedly set a $7.5 billion valuation for San Francisco-based TypeSafe. 3. Oratomic , $475M, quantum computing: Pasadena, California-based Oratomic, a startup working on fault-tolerant quantum computers, raised $475 million in fresh funding led by Arch Venture Partners , Spark Capital , Khosla Ventures , Index Ventures , General Catalyst and Bezos Expeditions . The company previously raised $300 million in a July financing. 4. SignSplit , $400M, data and content protection: SignSplit, a provider of tools for protecting, licensing and contributing real-world human data and other forms of human contribution, emerged from stealth with $400 million in seed funding. W Group backed the round, setting a $1 billion valuation for the New York-based company, which was founded in 2024. 5. (tied) Vinci , $250M, AI for engineering: Vinci, developer of an AI computational platform for hardware engineers to design products, closed on $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. Advent , Temasek and Xora led the round for the Palo Alto, California-based company. 5. (tied) Atomic Machines , $250M, micro-manufacturing: Emeryville, California-based Atomic Machines, a startup working on AI-native digital manufacturing systems to build micro-machines directly from code, emerged from stealth and said it has raised $250 million to date from a long list of investors. 7. Voltus , $225M, energy distribution: Voltus, provider of a distributed energy platform aimed at bolstering grid flexibility, picked up $225 million in Series D funding. Generation Investment Management , Activate Capital and Vitol led the financing for the San Francisco-based startup. 8. (tied) Type One Energy , $200M, fusion: Knoxville, Tennessee-based Type One Energy, a developer of fusion energy technology, secured $200 million in Series B financing led by Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Clutterbuck Capital . 8. (tied) Ledgebrook , $200M, insurance: Ledgebrook, an AI-powered specialty insurance platform, closed on $200 million in equity financing co-led by Allianz X and Rockefeller Capital Management . The round brings total funding to date for Boston-based Ledgebrook to around $315 million, per Crunchbase data . 8. (tied) Arena , $200M, AI evaluation: Arena, provider of a platform for evaluating AI models, pulled in $200 million in Series B funding and said it has exceeded a $100 million annual revenue run rate. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Khosla Ventures led the round, which set a $3.1 billion valuation for the company. title: Media
summary:
昨天发帖请大家提名最想平替的付费软件。今天交 Day 2 的账单和最终选题。

### 1. 为什么定下 Beyond Compare ？

昨晚到今天，AI 员工把 6 个平台的 134 条评论全抓回来了（ V2EX 占了 118 条）。

除去提名重写 Windows 11 、SAP 、MATLAB 和微信的老哥，呼声最高的实用工具就是 **Beyond Compare**。

大家苦它久矣：**Pro 版买断要 70 美金（约 500 元）**，跨大版本升级还要交半价。而 Mac 上的开源替代品 Meld 长期断更卡顿，KDiff3 的界面还停在二十年前。

除了评论区提名，AI 还去外网盲测了一圈，把取消买断改收 108 美金年费的录屏软件 `Screen Studio` 也拉进了决赛圈。
不过内部圆桌吵了两轮后，我还是在手机上拍板了 **Beyond Compare**，开源项目定名 **`OpenCompare`**。

![选品圆桌：两波调研 + 三席位两轮互搏的分工图]( https://media.munk.sh/blog/day-02/round-table.png)

原因很简单：一是听劝，兑现评论区最高票；二是它零外部依赖，做完直接丢测试文件夹、冲突代码和乱序表格进去，机器自己就能跑完桌面实机验收。

### 2. 5 个研发日，只做哪 4 件事？

去掉首尾，写代码加自测只有 5 天。为了不搞出个半吊子玩具，我们砍掉了十六进制对比、远端挂载和容易误删文件的双向同步，只死磕最常用的 4 个功能：

1. **双文件夹极速对比**：按大小、修改时间和哈希秒级比对，一键过滤出差异文件。
2. **代码双栏对比与三向合并**：遇到 Git 冲突时，摆清三方冲突块，点一下就能采纳并导出。
3. **千行 CSV 按主键列对齐对比**：这是普通编辑器内置 Diff 最抓瞎的地方。两份乱序表格，指定一列当主键（比如订单号），自动拉齐每一行并高亮改过的单元格。

### 3. 今日 Token 账单与一次断流

- **DeepSeek （执行员工）**：12.50M Tokens
- **缓存命中率**：**89.4%**（共命中 31.92M 缓存，所以实际花费很稳）

![Day 2 本机 Token 用量截图：35.69M （ Gemini 23.19M + DeepSeek 12.5M ）]( https://media.munk.sh/blog/day-02/tokens.png)

后来，我仔细分析了一下，原来是我的系统有 bug ，Sub Agent 会默认继承 Supervisor 的模型。从明天开始，模型用量比例应该能有所下降。

今晚 Gemini 4 已经开始搭桌面端架子和对比内核。明天 **Day 3**，带第一批代码提交和跑起来的真实窗口来交作业。大家平时用 BC 最看重哪个细节，欢迎继续提！

title: RDST
summary: A local agent that watches Postgres/MySQL for query regressions

extra.author: gvsg
extra.original_title: Show HN: RDST – A local agent that watches Postgres/MySQL for query regressions

story_text.value:
We noticed during the course of many many years of DBA related work that fixes to database issues and queries are always reactive. An entire database can fall over extremely quickly when an unbounded query grows without warning.

Traditionally, DBAs hear complaints of slowness and follow a methodical process: - manually browse pg_stats or other database related performance internal tables - see which queries are slowest - figure out what indexes are missing - figure out which indexes are actually bad and slowing down writes - painstakingly implement a fix

In the age of cheap intelligence, we decided that there is no reason we can’t have an always-on agent that is designed to do this job for you. Databases need something or someone that is always watching with a massive amount of contextual understanding to be able to take quick actions. We’ve watched the alternative play out repeatedly. One of our users’s checkout page went from loading instantly to taking 11 seconds in a single night with no code change. How? Well somehow their order table grew by 40M rows because BI team had injected historical data and suddenly postgres started doing full table scans. Sometimes routine operations have unintended results and can easily destroy your database. We wanted to catch these kinds of regressions instantly. So we built RDST.

RDST is a desktop agent that runs on your PC and connects to PostgreSQL / MYSQL (read only) and compares every query against its own performance every minute. Every expensive query is automatically EXPLAIN ANALYZED, stripped of PII and sent to U.S. based frontier or open model providers to analyze which indexes are missing, how the query could be rewritten, and provides the fix. We then run a classifier model (JEV) to decide if you should be notified (is this standard behavior for this particular query?), and the full history of the query performance is kept for years. RDST also keeps track of your entire database health in general, and recommends more fixes than simply bad queries.

Since it runs locally we can keep the database credentials stored in your OS Keychain (RDST never keeps them in its own storage layer), and the connection goes straight to your database (using a jump host or SSH tunnel for private connections). You can read more about how we handle data especially as it pertains to LLM use here.

https://readyset.io/docs/readyset-ai/rdst/desktop/privacy

We really want feedback from the community from people running Postgres and MySQL in production. We are giving inference away completely for free.

Just as a reminder, RDST will NOT run any updates or indexes against your database at this time. We are considering a fully autonomous auto-pilot mode in the future, but for now we are leaving the actual fixes in your hands.

Let us know what you think!

title: BookPress
summary: a WordPress core in C/C++ (Live Demo)

extra.author: squareys
extra.original_title: Show HN: BookPress, a WordPress core in C/C++ (Live Demo)

story_text.value:
Since ~40% of all websites supposedly still run on WordPress (WP), I thought it might be useful to run it faster. BookPress is about 50% faster than a performance-tuned WP setup with Elementor and WooCommerce.

Every time I used WordPress in the past, I got frustrated how slow it was, even with just a few plugins. So I wrote an light-weight C/C++ core and an embeddable PHP engine to run plugins and themes, with most of the WP API surface covered.

Try the live demo, including wp-admin!

The embeddable PHP runtime that covers most of Zend PHP's features runs 2x slower than Zend, but BookPress is still faster than a performance-tuned WP instance with OPCache, page cache and object caches.

BookPress runs alongside a traditional WP installation on Linux arm64 and x86_64.

Looking forward to what you all think.

title: My Terminal Themes Web App
summary: Well, after 15 years of saying "Someday I'll turn this into a web app," I finally did it! I've been maintaining a popular repo of terminal themes at https://github.com/mbadolato/iT…

extra.author: bado
extra.original_title: Show HN: My Terminal Themes Web App

story_text.value:
Well, after 15 years of saying "Someday I'll turn this into a web app," I finally did it!

I've been maintaining a popular repo of terminal themes at https://github.com/mbadolato/iTerm2-Color-Schemes, and it was finally time to build the app with all the features I wanted!

So, the next-gen version is live at https://terminalthemes.com! It currently has over 800 themes, and provides downloads for close to 40 different formats (iTerm, Ghostty, Windows, and many more)

It's free for everyone. An account is not needed to browse and download, but registering for an account (free) allows you to vote, bookmark, submit themes, etc.

I focused on a11y features for those who need it, in addition to adding Find My Theme and other tools to make it easy to find something you like!

Live terminal and code previews help show a more realistic view of the terminal, as opposed to the ANSI screenshots used at the GitHub repository. Those are still there, for those who like them.

I would love for you guys to check it out and provide feedback, feature suggestions, whatever!

And a huge thanks to the community of people that have contributed themes, ports to other terminals, and tools to provide conversions between formats over the years.

Oh! And if you've ever contributed themes to the GitHub repo, please register for an account, find your theme(s), and hit the Claim Authorship button!

title: Ito
summary: Build Terminal UIs in Lua

extra.author: cat-whisperer
extra.original_title: Show HN: Ito – Build Terminal UIs in Lua

story_text.value:
My friend and I are huge Neovim nerds. We like to rice our terminals and our editors. We just wanted a harness that we can do the same with, rice it till our hearts' desire. So, we started looking out for harnesses. Pi was great, Pi was good. But in the end, it was JavaScript. I don't have anything against JavaScript, but Lua is more fitting, and I can just as easily base it in Rust to make it even faster. So, we started cooking, and we ended up with a design that's minimal at its core and is built using Lua. Every built-in abstraction, the way you define providers, the way you rice it up, everything, literally everything, you can do in Lua.

But how? How does it all work? I proposed we just do it the Ratatui way, but my friend was like, nah! We shall make it possible to build TUIs in Lua. (Weirdo!) But it paid off, and we got ourselves a shiny new Lua library, ito!!!

He didn't get the gravity of the situation. We had an awesome terminal UI library in Lua! I wanted everyone to know how cool that is, so I got cooking, wrote myself a custom canvas implementation of this library instead of the usual terminal adaptor, exported it as wasm, and made this super cool website where you can experiment building awesome UIs in Lua. For vibe-coders, we got an llms.txt too. Have at it, and see if you can build something really cool with it. The library's at github.com/uji-labs/ito, and the awesome sauce harness is at github.com/uji-labs/uji.

I hope you like it!

story_text.value:
There are many movies and shows out there with neither subtitles or dubs in English (or any other language). Pretty much impossible to watch.

With SOTA AI now directing the process, you can do it locally on your machine. You basically just clone the repo, open up Codex or Claude and tell it to dub the video you want in the language you want.

The repo contains all the scripts and guidance I've developed over the past few weeks to create dubs that are watchable, as an added bonus the voices in the dub are the actors own voices which is really nice.

Also it's self improving, each dub may modify the scripts for better fidelity. So feel free to push them back to the repo so everyone benefits. Thanks.

title: Petal
summary: open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free

extra.author: thedracle
extra.original_title: Show HN: Petal, open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen.

As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st.

Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal (https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal)

Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry.

Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017.

When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.”

Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server. We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration. So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle.

We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector. What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around. It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to. The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here. Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

title: clova
summary: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox

extra.author: edpin2000
extra.original_title: Show HN: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox

story_text.value:
Infinite inboxes, including prefixes where you don't have to create inboxes before you use them -- they self create when you add a suffix.

Three types of inboxes: - One sender. Locks to the first domain to send email (except gmail, outlook, etc where it locks to an email account for obivous reasons. It bounces everyone else. - Temporary. Lasts for a while (24h, 7days, etc) then bounces. Received messages stay or go as per your choice. - Prefix. The most powerful. Declare a prefix like "service" and then invent any suffix, like "service-netflix" or "service$bank" and it creates a new one-sender inbox locked to whoever wrote first.

Bring you own domain. Bring your own AI (MCP server ready). Forwarding.

Please help me test it.
